title: Word Abbreviation
statement:
You are given an array `words` of distinct strings. Return an array holding the shortest abbreviation of each word under the rules below, in the same order as `words`.

- Keeping the first `k` letters of a word gives the abbreviation made of those `k` letters, then the number of letters that sit between them and the word's last letter (written in decimal), then the last letter. For example, `"apple"` with `k = 1` becomes `"a3e"`, and with `k = 2` becomes `"ap2e"`.
- Every word starts with `k = 1`.
- While some abbreviation is shared by two or more words, all of those words increase their `k` by one and are abbreviated again. This repeats until every word's abbreviation is unique.
- Whenever an abbreviation would not be strictly shorter than its word, the word itself is used instead.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters
All strings in words are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Words contain no digits, so an abbreviation reads back unambiguously: two words can only share one if they have the same length, the same last letter and the same kept prefix. The greedy idea is to give every word its shortest abbreviation first and lengthen only the words that are actually in a clash, all of them together, exactly as the rules say. A brute force would rerun whole rounds over every word until nothing is shared; here each word is settled in turn instead.

Checking only the words after `i` is enough. A word grows only while it clashes, so any word whose prefix is still shorter than word `i`'s already differs from it inside that shorter prefix. Once `i` has no clash with a later word, nothing can ever match it again.

## Approach

1. `abbreviate(word, keep)` returns the word itself when `keep >= word.length - 2` (the result would not be shorter); otherwise it joins the first `keep` letters, the count of letters skipped, and the last letter.
2. Start every `prefix` at 1 and fill `result` with those first abbreviations.
3. For each `i`, collect every later `j` whose abbreviation equals `result[i]` into `clashes`.
4. If there are none, word `i` is final; move on.
5. Otherwise add `i` itself, grow the `prefix` of every word in `clashes` by one, re-abbreviate them, and check `i` again.
6. Return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

The first abbreviations are `l2e`, `god` (kept whole: `g1d` is no shorter), `i6l`, `me`, `i6t`, `i6l`, `i7n`, `f2e`, `i7n`.

- `internal` clashes with `interval` on `i6l`. Both grow to `in5l`, `int4l`, `inte3l`, `inter2l`; at `keep = 6` neither abbreviation is shorter, so both stay whole and now differ.
- `intension` clashes with `intrusion` on `i7n`. They grow through `in6n` and `int5n` and split at `inte4n` and `intr4n`.
- Every other word is already unique, giving `["l2e","god","internal","me","i6t","interval","inte4n","f2e","intr4n"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(C²), where C is the total number of letters: `prefix[i]` grows at most `word.length` times, and each round compares and rebuilds the later words. In practice most string comparisons stop at the first letter.
- Space: O(C) for the abbreviations.

## Pitfalls

- When a clash happens, **every** word in it grows, including `i` itself; growing only the later ones leaves the others too short.
- A word stays whole when the abbreviation is not strictly shorter: every word of length 2 or 3, and any word once `keep` reaches `length - 2`.
- The middle count can have several digits (`characterization` becomes `c14n`), so append the number, not a single character.
- Words of different lengths or last letters never clash, even when their first letters match.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `abbreviate(word, keep)` | the abbreviation keeping `keep` leading letters, or the word itself |
| `prefix[i]` | how many leading letters word `i` currently keeps |
| `result[i]` | word `i`'s current abbreviation |
| `i` | the word being made unique |
| `clashes` | indices of the words sharing `result[i]`, then `i` too |
| `index` | one word of the clash being lengthened |

narration.3: If the abbreviation would not be shorter than the word, use the word itself.
narration.4: Join the kept letters, the number of skipped letters and the last letter.
narration.7: Every word starts by keeping just its first letter.
narration.9: Make the words unique one at a time, in order.
narration.10: Repeat until word i shares its abbreviation with no later word.
narration.12: Look at every word after i.
narration.13: Record each later word with exactly the same abbreviation.
narration.15: No clash left: word i's abbreviation is final.
narration.16: Word i is part of the clash as well.
narration.17: Lengthen every word in the clash together.
narration.19: Rebuild its abbreviation with the longer prefix.
narration.23: Every abbreviation is now unique and as short as the rules allow.
